source_text:
In sanctos martyres (fragmentum) (homilia 17) [Dub.]
̔Ησυχίου, ἀπὸ ἐγκωμίων εἰς μάρτυρας.
1 Ὑμεῖς οὖν, ἄνδρες ἀδελφοὶ καὶ πατέρες, τὸν πολυανθῆ κῆπον εἰσελθόντες
τοῦ Πνεύματος προθύμως ἐκεῖθεν τὰς ἀρετὰς τρυγήσατε, μὴ μίαν ἀλλὰ πολλάς,
μᾶλλον δὲ μὴ πολλὰς ἀλλὰ πάσας· ἀρετὴ γὰρ ἀρετῆς χρῄζει, ἐπειδὴ καὶ πτεροῦ
πτερὸν καὶ τροχοῦ τροχὸς καὶ βαθμὸς βαθμίδος καὶ κώπη κώπης καὶ πηδαλίου
πηδάλιον. Ἐὰν μὴ ζεύξῃς λίθῳ λίθον, ὁ πύργος εἰς ὕψος οὐκ ἐγήγερται· τὸν αὐτὸν δὴ
τρόπον, ἐὰν μὴ νόμον ἐπὶ νόμον κατορθώσωμεν, τὸν οὐρανὸν οὐ φθάνομεν· ἐὰν μὴ
συνάψῃς ἐντολὴν ἐντολῇ, ἀτελὴς ὁ δρόμος.
thought_title: Enter the Spirit's garden and gather all virtues
orientation: The preacher opens his encomium by calling the congregation to enter the Spirit's garden and gather every virtue, not just one.
pass_a_gloss: You therefore, men brothers and fathers, having entered the many-flowered garden of the Spirit, eagerly from there gather the virtues, not one but many, rather not many but all; for virtue needs virtue, since also wing needs wing and wheel needs wheel and step needs step and oar needs oar and rudder needs rudder. If you do not join stone to stone, the tower has not been raised to height; in the same way indeed, if we do not set commandment upon commandment aright, we do not reach heaven; if you do not join commandment to commandment, the course is incomplete.

choices.why: Literal rendering of the compound adjective; keeps the image of a garden rich in blooms as the source of virtues.
The verb means to harvest or pick fruit; 'gather' preserves the agricultural image without narrowing to grapes.
Simple and direct; the verb expresses requirement or lack.
The verb means to yoke or join together; 'join' fits the building image of a tower.
The verb means to accomplish or set upright; 'set aright' captures the moral sense of fulfilling law upon law.
δρόμος means a running course or race; 'course' keeps the athletic metaphor, and 'incomplete' renders ἀτελής literally.

pass_b_english: So then, brothers and fathers, enter the Spirit's many-flowered garden and eagerly gather the virtues from it—not one, but many; or rather, not many, but all of them. For virtue needs virtue, just as wing needs wing, wheel needs wheel, step needs step, oar needs oar, and rudder needs rudder. If you do not join stone to stone, the tower will not rise to a height. In the same way, if we do not set commandment upon commandment, we will not reach heaven; if you do not join commandment to commandment, the course is incomplete.

last_rejected.why: Glossary requires 'commandment' for ἐντολή, but νόμος is not in glossary; however 'law' here is ambiguous. More critically, 'set aright' obscures that κατορθόω means to fulfill/perform rightly, and 'law' for νόμος in this context likely means commandment/ordinance.
last_rejected.fix: if we do not fulfill commandment upon commandment, we will not reach heaven
last_rejected.ruling: κατορθόσωμεν means 'set aright/succeed'; νόμος as 'law' is standard. No meaning lost; glossary not broken.

problems.quote: if we do not set aright law upon law, we will not reach heaven
problems.why: Mixed singular/plural and odd metaphor; 'set aright law upon law' is not natural English.
problems.fix: Use 'if we do not set law upon law' or 'if you do not join law to law' for consistency.

edits.old: if we do not set aright law upon law, we will not reach heaven
edits.new: if we do not set law upon law, we will not reach heaven

fixed: Removed 'aright' to match the source's 'νόμον ἐπὶ νόμον' without adding an interpretive adverb.

problems.why: Same Greek concept (nomos/entole) rendered two ways in one paragraph

edits.old: if we do not set law upon law, we will not reach heaven
edits.new: if we do not set commandment upon commandment, we will not reach heaven

fixed: Changed 'law upon law' to 'commandment upon commandment' in both the English and the literal gloss to use 'commandment' consistently for νόμον and ἐντολήν.
